entry.title: Ainu anchi-piri
entry.summary: Hokkaido and Sakhalin: a woman's mouth ringed with indigo, begun in childhood and widened until she was ready to marry.

entry.title: Amazigh marks
entry.summary: North Africa: women's chin, forehead and hand marks, in a geometric vocabulary shared with weaving and pottery.

entry.title: Atayal ptasan
entry.summary: Taiwan: a band down the forehead, and a second mark earned — by a man for taking a head, by a woman for mastering the loom.

entry.title: Batok
entry.summary: The Philippine traditions, tapped with a hafted thorn at ninety to a hundred and twenty strikes a minute.

entry.title: Chin facial tattooing
entry.summary: Women's faces, marked between fifteen and twenty, in a pattern that names the tribe: full-face, part-face, dots, lines, or both.

entry.title: The pilgrim's cross
entry.summary: Jerusalem and Egypt: a cross on the inside of the wrist, marking a pilgrimage — and a family that has been doing it for around seven hundred years.

entry.title: Deq
entry.summary: Kurdistan: marks on women's faces, hands and feet, for protection, for health, and to say which tribe.

entry.title: Derung face marks
entry.summary: Yunnan: Derung women marked on the face at twelve or thirteen, in a tradition now carried by a handful of elders.

entry.title: Godna
entry.summary: Northern and central India: women's marks, pricked by women, carried out of India to the Caribbean by indentured labour.

entry.title: Hajichi
entry.summary: The Ryukyu Islands: marks on the backs of women's hands, outlawed by Japan in 1899 and now being put back on.

entry.title: Hlai women's marks
entry.summary: Hainan: Hlai women marked on face, throat, arms and legs in patterns that told one lineage from another.

entry.title: Htoe kwin
entry.summary: Every up-country Burmese man wore one: a sheet of dark-blue animals from the navel to below the knee, begun in boyhood.

entry.title: Iban tattooing
entry.summary: Borneo: tapped designs carved on a block and printed onto the skin, with hand marks reserved for a man who had taken a head.

entry.title: Irezumi
entry.summary: Japan: needles bound with silk to a wooden rod, worked by hand — *tebori*, carving by hand — over years, in a design that covers the body like a garment.

entry.title: Kakiniit
entry.summary: Inuit tattoos: women's work on women's skin, stitched with a sooted thread drawn under the skin, or poked.

entry.title: Cordilleran whatok
entry.summary: The Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, where Spanish rule never reached and the tattooing was never interrupted.

entry.title: Kayan tattooing
entry.summary: Upriver Borneo, where the tattooists were women and the work went on a woman's forearms, thighs and feet across years.

entry.title: Konyak marks
entry.summary: Nagaland and across the Myanmar border: chest and face marks a man received for taking a head.

entry.title: Patutiki
entry.summary: The Marquesas: coverage so complete that Willowdean Handy's 1922 survey had to be drawn panel by panel to record it.

entry.title: Mentawai titi
entry.summary: The Mentawai islands, west of Sumatra: long lines laid along arms, chest and legs, added to at each stage of a life.

entry.title: Sak kha lai
entry.summary: The Lanna leg tattoo: waist to knee, sometimes to the ankle, dense enough that the murals paint it as a pair of black trousers.

entry.title: Sak yant
entry.summary: Letters, numbers and figures arranged into a diagram — *yant* — and pricked into skin with a long needle.

entry.title: Shan leg tattooing
entry.summary: The same leg work as the Burmese, carried further — to the ankles, up the back, and on the specialists who tattooed everybody else's charms.

entry.title: Sicanje
entry.summary: Bosnia: Catholic girls' forearms and hands marked with crosses, circles and fences, pricked with soot and honey.

entry.title: Stick and poke
entry.summary: The one everybody has seen: a needle, ink, no machine — punk kitchens, prisons, and now studios that do nothing else.

entry.title: Tā moko
entry.summary: New Zealand: albatross-bone chisels struck with a mallet, cutting a groove that stays visible as texture, not only as colour.

entry.title: Tatau
entry.summary: Samoa: a comb of bone and turtle shell, struck with a mallet, covering a man from the middle of the back to the knees.

entry.title: Veiqia
entry.summary: Fiji: girls marked at puberty by older women called *dauveiqia*, paid in tapa cloth and whale teeth.

entry.title: Cut
entry.summary: The skin is cut or chiselled and pigment is rubbed into the cut, so the mark has a texture as well as a colour.

entry.title: Machine
entry.summary: An electric motor drives the needle, at speeds between fifty and three thousand insertions a minute. It is here for contrast.

entry.title: Poke
entry.summary: A point held in the hand and pushed into the skin, once per mark, with the pigment carried on or into the hole.

entry.title: Stitch
entry.summary: A needle carrying a thread blackened with soot, drawn through the skin so the line of pigment stays where the thread passed.

entry.title: Tap
entry.summary: A needle or a comb of needles fixed at a right angle to a handle, and a second piece of wood striking the handle to drive it in.

entry.title: Au
entry.summary: A set of combs — wide ones for filling, narrow ones for line — each hafted at a right angle and struck with a light mallet.

entry.title: The design block
entry.summary: Not a needle: a carved wooden block, inked and printed onto the skin, so the tattooist follows a line instead of remembering one.

entry.title: Gisi and pat-ik
entry.summary: A citrus thorn — or a bundle of them — lashed at a right angle to a short stick, tapped by a second stick.

entry.title: Hnitkwasok
entry.summary: A brass rod about two feet long, weighted at the top with a cast figure, with a split four-way point at the other end.

entry.title: Khem sak
entry.summary: The sak yant needle: a long steel or brass shaft, pushed with one hand and steered with the other.

entry.title: Lek char
entry.summary: The northern instrument: an iron stylus of the kind used to incise palm-leaf manuscripts, taken to skin.

entry.title: Needle and sinew
entry.summary: The same needle that sewed the clothing, threaded with sinew blackened in soot and drawn under the skin.
